name: Museum Het Schip
overview: Museum of the Amsterdam School in the former school of the Het Schip housing block at Oostzaanstraat 45, in the Spaarndammerbuurt of Amsterdam (museum's site; English Wikipedia).
Michel de Klerk designed the block, built in 1919 for the housing corporation Eigen Haard, which still owns it (museum's site). The museum has been there since 2001 (English Wikipedia).
The name Het Schip, "The Ship", comes from the building's shape (museum's site).
funding_verdict: Museum Het Schip: mainly public and housing-association money: Amsterdams Fonds voor de Kunst (AFK), the Amsterdam housing associations' federation and earned income

press_items.title: AT5, "Voortbestaan van Amsterdams museum Het Schip bedreigd door wegvallen subsidie" (2020)

name: W139
overview: Artist-driven production and presentation space for contemporary art at Warmoesstraat 139, in central Amsterdam (W139 contact page).

Founded in 1979 when a group of artists squatted the building. Wikipedia says five young artists squatted the former theatre in October 1979 as "a movement against the closed world of commercial art and museums".
The name W139 is the street address.
funding_verdict: W139: mainly public: Amsterdam and national arts funds, with private funds and own income
wider_context: An open letter signed "Collective Refusal", from artists, cultural workers and publics, "demands the removal of Art Rotterdam from Ahoy" and an "ethical realignment" of the Mondriaan Fund's commitments, and objects to the fund hosting Prospects at Ahoy in 2026. The page describes NEDS, an arms fair held at Ahoy for 35 years, and names Elbit Systems and Lockheed Martin as exhibitors in 2023 and 2024 (Dutch Art Institute, undated page, no named author; advocacy source).
The Mondriaan Fund gives W139 structural support for 2025 to 2028. The letter names the fund, Art Rotterdam and Ahoy; it does not mention W139.

name: Cultuurhuis Bergeijk
overview: Museum at Domineestraat 8a in Bergeijk that runs tours of Gerrit Rietveld's Van Daalen House. The tour starts at the De Ploeg monument, Riethovensedijk 20, about a 10-minute walk from the house (Cultuurhuis site).
Formed in 2021 by merging the foundations Eicha, Rietveld & Ruys and Bezoekerscentrum Teutenhuis (Cultuurhuis site).
The house is named for the Van Daalen family: Roelof van Daalen, co-director of the weaving firm De Ploeg, commissioned it (tour page).
funding_verdict: Cultuurhuis Bergeijk: mainly public: the Municipality of Bergeijk, with Friends, a lottery fund and own sales

name: Van Doesburg-Rinsemahuis
overview: Museum house at Torenstraat 3 in Drachten, run with Museum Dr8888 at Museumplein 2 (museum site).

In 1921 municipal architect Cees Rienks de Boer designed sixteen middle-class houses and a school for Smallingerland. Theo van Doesburg, brought in through the Drachten shoemaker Evert Rinsema, designed the colour scheme of the neighbourhood later nicknamed the Papegaaienbuurt, the parrot neighbourhood (Herenhuis, Dutch Wikipedia).
Named for Van Doesburg and the shoemaker brothers and amateur artists Evert and Thijs Rinsema (museum site).
funding_verdict: Van Doesburg-Rinsemahuis: mainly public: municipal and provincial subsidy through Museum Dr8888

press_items.title: Natascha Drabbe, "De Stijl in Drachten" in the series "Iconische huizen in Nederland" (2022)

name: Jachthuis Sint Hubertus
overview: Country house and museum at Houtkampweg 9 in Otterlo, inside the Hoge Veluwe National Park, which has entrances at Otterlo, Schaarsbergen and Hoenderloo (Iconic Houses, Park site).
H.P. Berlage designed it for Anton and Helene Kröller-Müller. It was completed in 1920 after disagreements between Berlage and Helene delayed construction (Park site).
Named after St. Hubertus (English Wikipedia). The Kröllers used it mainly as a country house and lived there permanently only in their last years (Park site).
funding_verdict: Jachthuis Sint Hubertus: mainly visitor income to the Park foundation, with State-paid maintenance and corporate partners

name: Cuypershuis
overview: Museum about the architect Pierre Cuypers in his former home and studio at Pierre Cuypersstraat 1, Roermond (museum site).
Built in 1853 as Cuypers's home and studio. The firm Cuypers & Stolzenberg worked there, designing neo-Gothic buildings with more than 80 employees, until work ended in 1947 (Dutch Wikipedia).

Named for Cuypers. Princess Juliana opened the municipal museum, first the Gemeentelijk Museum Hendrik Luyten-Dr. Cuypers and later the Stedelijk Museum Roermond, in the building on 23 August 1932, and it stayed until 2009 (Dutch Wikipedia).
funding_verdict: Cuypershuis: mainly public: the municipality of Roermond, with a friends foundation and gifts

name: Kijk-Kubus
overview: Furnished show cube at Overblaak 70 in Piet Blom's Cube Houses, in the east of Rotterdam's city centre near Blaak station, the Market Hall, the library and the Old Harbour (stated by the museum).
Ed R. de Graaf founded it, and the site says it opens this year for its 42nd season (stated by the museum).

Piet Blom designed the Cube Houses, built from 1982 to 1984 after plans were first shown in 1978: 38 cube houses and 13 business cubes on the Overblaak pedestrian viaduct, a municipal monument known as the Blaakse Bos, the Blaak Forest (Dutch Wikipedia).
funding_verdict: Kijk-Kubus: self-funded: ticket income for a small private foundation

name: Sonneveld House
overview: Museum house at Jongkindstraat 12 in Rotterdam, on the edge of Museumpark and a short walk from the Nieuwe Instituut's museum building (Nieuwe Instituut, annual report 2025).
Brinkman and Van der Vlugt designed it for Albertus Sonneveld, a director of the Van Nelle factory. Construction began in 1932 and the family moved in during 1933 (Nieuwe Instituut, Dutch Wikipedia).
Named for the Sonneveld family. After Sonneveld sold in 1956, Belgium used it as a consulate-general until 1996 (Dutch Wikipedia).
funding_verdict: Sonneveld House: mainly public: the Ministry of Education, Culture and Science (OCW) through Het Nieuwe Instituut

name: V2_ Lab for the Unstable Media
overview: Lab for art, technology and society at Eendrachtsstraat 10, off Witte de Withstraat in central Rotterdam, a 15 minute walk from Rotterdam Centraal Station (V2_ contact page).
Founded in 1981 as an artist collective in a squat at Vughterstraat 234 in 's-Hertogenbosch, hence the name V2_. Founding members included Alex Adriaansens and Joke Brouwer (V2_ history page).
It issued the "Manifesto for Unstable Media" in 1987, moved to its current location in Rotterdam in 1994, and opened the V2_Lab media laboratory in May 1998 (V2_ history page).
funding_verdict: V2_ Lab for the Unstable Media: public structural funding from the Creative Industries Fund NL and the City of Rotterdam, plus EU project money and Dutch foundations

name: Huis Jan de Jong
overview: House and office of the architect Jan de Jong (1917 to 2001) at Rijksweg 56, Schaijk, on a private estate with four connected courtyards and gardens (Hendrick de Keyser).

De Jong built it in stages. Hendrick de Keyser dates a walled front garden and gazebo to 1956, the current house with its office wing to 1967 and 1968, an entrance court to about 1976 and the last extensions to the 1980s. The Jan de Jong Stichting dates the house to 1962 to 1967.
Named for De Jong. Hendrick de Keyser gives 2016 as the year it acquired the house, the Jan de Jong Stichting gives March 2017. It became a Rijksmonument in February 2019 (Jan de Jong Stichting).
funding_verdict: Huis Jan de Jong: owned by Vereniging Hendrick de Keyser: rents and services, bequests, the VriendenLoterij and subsidies, with a yearly deficit

name: Kunstmuseum Den Haag
overview: Municipal art museum in The Hague, home to the largest Mondriaan collection in the world (City of The Hague), and, according to Wikipedia, Mondrian's last work, Victory Boogie-Woogie.

Founded on 29 May 1866 by a group of artists and collectors as the Museum voor Moderne Kunst. It was known as the Haags Gemeentemuseum until 1998 and as Gemeentemuseum Den Haag until September 2019 (Wikipedia).
The building was designed by H.P. Berlage and built from 1931 to 1935. Berlage died in 1934 and his son-in-law E.E. Strasser finished the work (Wikipedia).
funding_verdict: Kunstmuseum Den Haag: the City of The Hague, with a lottery, public funds and private funds

name: Stroom Den Haag
overview: Centre for contemporary art in the public domain at Hogewal 1 in central The Hague. It describes itself as an expertise centre for art, society and the public domain (stated by the space).
Dutch Wikipedia dates its founding to 1989. Stroom's own site says it has operated since 1990. It handles non-museum visual arts policy in The Hague (Wikipedia).
The name is not explained in the pages read.
funding_verdict: Stroom Den Haag: mainly public: the Municipality of The Hague

name: West Den Haag
overview: Contemporary art institution at Lange Voorhout 102 in The Hague's Museum Quarter, near the Binnenhof and about a 10-minute walk from The Hague Central Station (denhaag.com).

The building is the former United States embassy, designed by the Hungarian-American architect Marcel Breuer and completed in 1959. It is a national monument, and denhaag.com compares its windows and facade to the MET Breuer in New York.
Its programme pairs exhibitions with lectures, performances and discussions (denhaag.com).
funding_verdict: West Den Haag: public: city, national ministry and national arts infrastructure

name: De Pont
overview: Museum of contemporary art in a former wool-spinning mill in Tilburg, North Brabant (Dutch Wikipedia; museum website).
Founded by the Stichting De Pont, a foundation set up in 1988 with part of the estate of Jan de Pont. The museum opened on 12 September 1992 (Dutch Wikipedia; museum website).
Named for the lawyer and businessman J.H. (Jan) de Pont, born in Tilburg on 22 February 1915, who died there on 18 September 1987 (museum website).
funding_verdict: De Pont: self-funded: the bequest of Jan de Pont's estate, with no government subsidy

name: Van Schijndel House
overview: House at Pieterskerkhof 8 in the old centre of Utrecht, built on an inner courtyard behind the houses and gardens of the Pieterskerkhof and the Kromme Nieuwegracht, and largely hidden from the street (DUIC, 2016; Iconic Houses).

The architect Mart van Schijndel (1943 to 1999) bought the former Stichtse Glashandel in 1988, built the house inside the walls of its old business hall from 1992 and finished it in 1993 (DUIC, 2016; Iconic Houses). He designed it for himself and lived there with his wife, the architectural historian Natascha Drabbe, until his death on 30 September 1999 (DUIC, 2024).
He turned the 1939 gatehouse in front, designed by J.F. Berghoef as a garage with living space, into four postmodern apartments with a pink-and-white striped front (DUIC, 2016 and 2024).
funding_verdict: Van Schijndel House: self-funded: tour donations and friends' gifts to a volunteer-run foundation in a privately lived-in house

name: Christchurch Art Gallery
overview: Public art gallery, Christchurch Art Gallery Te Puna o Waiwhetū, at the corner of Worcester Boulevard and Montreal Street (gallery about page). Wikipedia says the Christchurch City Council funds and owns it.

Opened on 10 May 2003, replacing the Robert McDougall Art Gallery, which opened in 1932 in the Botanic Gardens with a £25,000 gift from Robert E. McDougall and closed on 16 June 2002 (gallery history page).
The council committed $5 million in 1995 to acquire a site, and bought the former Sheraton Hotel site in 1996 (gallery history page).
funding_verdict: Christchurch Art Gallery: mainly public: Christchurch City Council, plus a foundation and corporate partners

press_items.title: Gina Irish, "Exhibitions Christchurch" (issue 108; the page gives no date, and the content points to 2003)

name: G.A.S. Foundation (Guest Artists Space)
overview: Non-profit cultural centre with two sites: an urban hub in Oniru, Lagos, and a 54-acre farm, Ecology Green Farm, in Ijebu, Ogun State (BusinessDay, 2022).
Founded in 2019 by the artist Yinka Shonibare, who modelled it on Guest Projects, his London residency programme where artists work in his studio for a month (The Art Newspaper, 2019).

Lagos building: a brutalist-inspired structure around a central courtyard with live-work flats and a flexible project and exhibition space, designed by the architect Elsie Owusu with Nihinlola Shonibare (BusinessDay).
funding_verdict: G.A.S. Foundation: philanthropy-funded: Shonibare's UK foundation, individual patrons, art foundations and corporate partners including Still Earth Holdings, whose subsidiaries include an oil drilling contractor

name: KaviarFactory
overview: A private kunsthall for contemporary art in a former caviar factory, a concrete building from the 1950s on the edge of the sea in the fishing village of Henningsvær in Lofoten (Arterritory).
The Oslo collectors Venke and Rolf Hoff acquired the building after the cannery closed in 2006 (Arterritory); it opened on 9 June 2013 (Visit Lofoten).

The façade sign is a permanent work by the German artist Michael Sailstorfer, with the letters ART missing from KAVIARFACTORY, and the door handles are by Bjarne Melgaard (Arterritory, Visit Lofoten).
funding_verdict: KaviarFactory: private: the Hoff family's own money, plus ticket and shop sales

name: Pikene på Broen (Barents Spektakel, Terminal B Kunsthall)
overview: A collective of curators and producers in Kirkenes, 15 km from the Russian border and 50 km from the Finnish border (Pikene på Broen).

Bente Synnøve Andersen, Svea Andersen, Anne Mette Bjørgan, Inger Blix Kvammen and Solvor Vefsnmo set it up as an independent group in 1996; it became a limited company in 2001 (Pikene på Broen), registered on 3 April 2001 (Brønnøysund Register).

It runs the festival Barents Spektakel, first held in 2004, the residency programme BAR International, and Terminal B, its project space, gallery, art shop and office on the pedestrian street in central Kirkenes since 2017 (Pikene på Broen).
funding_verdict: Pikene på Broen: mainly public: the Ministry of Culture, the three northern counties and Sør-Varanger Municipality, plus yearly project grants

name: Riddu Riđđu
overview: An annual international Indigenous music and culture festival in Olmmáivággi (Manndalen) in Gáivuotna (Kåfjord) Municipality, Nord-Troms (Riddu Riđđu).

Young people in Kåfjord started it in 1991 to turn shame about their Sea Sámi background into pride through music and culture; in the early years Sámi road signs were shot at and families split over it (Riddu Riđđu, translated by the atlas).

Since 1 January 2010 it has been run by the company Riddu Riđđu Festivála AS (Brønnøysund Register), which has five permanent staff, a year-round crew of 100 and about 170 volunteers at festival time; its address is the Centre for Northern Peoples in Manndalen (Riddu Riđđu, translated by the atlas).
funding_verdict: Riddu Riđđu: mainly public: the Sámi Parliament, Arts Council Norway, the Ministry of Culture, Troms County and Kåfjord Municipality
